What do you really need to mod in open discussions? Spam? Real specific illegal threats (as opposed to hypotheticals)? Doxing?

The worst I see coming at the mods of /v/opendiscussion is a sea of butt hurt reports from people are offended that someone has a differing opinion & who just don't get the idea of what open discussion is all about.

OK. Looking further into your rules:

  • No name calling. Reasonable as a rule, I could see some edge cases there, but that rule seems to be more clear cut. "SJW" seems like a 50-50. Are you calling someone a SJW, or are you referring to a group of people commonly referred to as SJW. I think in the later case, people are calling them SJWs to try and differentiate them from feminists or even radical feminists. Did I just break the rules here with my discussion of the term?

  • Be respectful - A good guideline but almost impossible to enforce in a clear fair manner.

  • No Trolling - Asking controversial questions and stirring up passions of disagreement is a long time favorite troll technique. But that also seems to be close to the heart of what /v/opendiscussion should be about. I don't see how you could ban that. About the only troll techniques that I could see as being against the rules is, posting the same damn comment or question over & over again to be annoying (but that might also fall under spamming), changing your username to be similar to another poster to sow confusion in discussion, playing the say one thing, then change what you stated so the people replying look bad... there may be other bad troll techniques, but the most common case of "trolling" dove tails too nicely into what this is about.

  • "Stay on Topic" - people are going to naturally drift off on side tangents, which is part of the beauty of open discussions. I am not sure how you are going to keep a rule like that. I guess I would think of that as more a guideline.

The other rules seem reasonable.

Military training exercises tend to be designed to prepare soldiers to react to aggression from a likely adversary by simulating the likely behavior and actions of the adversary in the event of a confrontation.

From a purely technical perspective, IDF’s apparent equation of cyber attacks from a motley crowd of laptop-equipped Hamas hackers with defending Israel against an attack by the fleet of highly advanced extraterrestrial invaders appears rather strained.

Military forces and the like conduct simulations with ridiculous scenarios to practice transferable skills on a semi-regular basis. Numerous North American bodies have conducted training simulations wherein the threat was that of a zombie apocalypse, and many even recommend particular "zombie preparedness kits" for the public because the kits are just as useful for the actual threats facing the population. It's just a way to engage peoples' attention.
